content: It's new and surprising to me that the unique typing property is a conjecture. I learn this from the blog. I am very ignorant to type theory so I want to ask how important this conjecture is for formalization.

I don't think it's remotely important for the formalisation of mathematics. My understanding is that Lean's type theory has all sorts of anomalies if you're interested in studying type theories for their own sake and that this can even put people off working with lean. I remember computer scientists telling me in 2017 all sorts of terrible things about the poor behaviour of lean's type theory with respect to stuff like subject reduction, quotients, definitional equality etc and how Leo should change things to fix these problems, and these complaints just seemed to me to be completely irrelevant to mathematics: me and some undergraduates had formalised the basic theory of schemes in lean and none of the other provers had done this, and I was thinking "well if we can do schemes we can do anything, and I don't even know what subject reduction is".

Kevin, when I first read about these issues in the era of purely human-written Lean, I agreed with your take that these were largely irrelevant to the rank and file doing mathematics in Lean. I think even today if you're talking about the direct effect this has on say Mathlib, this remains mostly true.

When agents are writing far more Lean than humans though, this shifts significantly. The problem here is that we'd really like verification of the kernel as hardening against rewarding hacking into kernel bugs. Even today this remains largely an unrealized fear, but I think it grows as inevitably the scale of these proofs increases and move into true theory building. It is not the case that type theories like Lean's are inherently unverifiable, but I would say that they require venturing out more into the realm of proof techniques that are active research. As an example, papers like Definitional Inversion, Without Normalisation are from as recently as this summer. You can argue that the kernel bugs that have been uncovered recently are implementation problems. I think that is true in some sense, but some of these (in my opinion that I know isn't as widely held here) are implementation problems that revolve around the fact that Lean having a complex metatheory makes it complex to correctly implement. (I would say fixes like lean4#14806 for instance fall into this category)

I think the most promising path forward is lean4#14977, which has been carefully crafted to improve these issues, but is very specific and practical about what needs to be changed to get properties like transitive defeq, a verifiable level comparison algorithm, and a nicer implementation of things like elimination rules for inductives that shifts some of this logic to elaboration.

As a data point, since the early days way before AI era, my trust towards Lean rests on that experts like Mario are still working for #leantt and lean4lean like projects and theories behind them. I would never trust a machine as the foundation of the building I live in, without knowing there are experts working relentlessly to figure out whether its building blocks are solid. And I would have my ears up when experts are talking about which building blocks need more work to be sure, even if that's out of my depth.

Somewhat opposite to what the blog and #general > Lean in the wild @ 💬 may suggest (there are logical gaps in Lean 3 type theory thesis that concern the community but are not widely known), section 2.4 of lean4lean paper explained the consequences of unique typing as Corollary 2.8 and stated clearly:

The reason Conjecture 2.7 and Conjecture 2.9 have been downgraded from theorems in (Carneiro, 2019) to conjectures here is because the proof has an error in one of the technical lemmas, and it remains to be seen if it is possible to salvage the proof.
......
We still have reasons to believe the conjectures here are true, but more work is needed to determine how to structure the proof by induction. In (Lennon-Bertrand, 2025), Lennon-Bertrand explores some of the landscape of proof approaches that could be applied here, based on similar work for MetaRocq. The proof of soundness is not impacted because there are alternative routes to construct the model that avoid unique typing (also described in (Carneiro, 2019)), but these conjectures are necessary in at least some form in order to prove the correctness of the typechecker (see section 3).

And more recent progress seems to be described in AI-assisted formalization of Π injectivity and uniqueness of typing for Lean’s kernel on AITP 2026. IIUC, the promising path seems to be proving pi injectivity( which implies uniqueness of typing) based on constructions similar to the ones for Rocq’s and Agda’s kernels but not directly transferrable, the required repairs are being explored and described near the end of the abstract.

Also note the good work by @Jeremy Chen on metalean:

Consequences include the elusive "definitional inversion", consisting of injectivity of type constructors (on the diagonal) and no-confusion (on the off-diagonal), uniqueness of typing, uniqueness of sorts, subject reduction, which are the same consequences as DIWN, but extended to work with Lean's type theory.
Isn't this now fixed by two commits in lean4lean, or is there more work left?
There are a couple of sorries there still, and AFAICT these sorries are false (as the paper by Mario and others shows)

The couple of sorries is basically the .const case, which is basically where all the work is. In L4L, .const includes inductive types, and the exact counterexample is for k-like reduction. See:

variable {x y : Type} (p : x = x) (q : x = y)

/-- info: Type -/
#guard_msgs in
#reduce (types := true) Eq.rec (motive := fun _ _ => Type 1) Type p

/-- info: q ▸ Type -/
#guard_msgs in
#reduce (types := true) Eq.rec (motive := fun _ _ => Type 1) Type q

In the domain model, x y p q are neutrals and are interpreted as ⊥\bot⊥. However, k-like reduction is allowed to inspect the variable names and deduce that, according to proof irrelevance, p can be replaced by refl, and thus compute. Since the model identifies all neutrals as ⊥\bot⊥, it is inadequate in this case. This was solved by the post I made here. It's also in metalean which has a full soundness proof, albeit for a slightly simplified theory

Just recently, I got to understand why unique typing is tricky. Maybe, it is well known for the people here but let me just share some examples how easily conflating definitional & structural equality breaks typing uniqueness.

Eta rule

  • Assume e : Empty.
    Under inconsistent context, every equality is True, se we can prove
    Empty = Nat
    and infer
    e : Nat
    (that is the step invalid in the typing system, but very natural). Then continue with
    Nat.succ e : Nat

Outside of the inconsistent context, this leads to:
(fun e : Empty => Nat.succ e) : (Empty → Nat)
which eta-reduces to:
Nat.succ : (Empty → Nat)
contradicting unique typing with the actual type of Nat.succ
(Lean can actually prove Empty → Nat differs from Nat → Nat).

Propositional extensionality.

By propext, all True propositions are equal, such as (True → True) = (∀ n : Nat, True). However, if we allow such rewrite in a type judgement, we could take a proof
(fun pf => pf) : (True → True)
and change it to
(fun pf => pf) : (∀ n : Nat, True)
Hence
(fun pf => pf) 5 : True
which beta-reduces to
5 : True

I know that conflating definitional & structural equality is quite a strong assumption, on the other hand, I think it is quite natural while actually modeling Lean (in set-theory, and similar systems). For example, I expect con-leche doesn't have type uniqueness, and rather unifies the equalities, right?
Yes, morally no unique typing in con-leche because of that.

An example I find even more striking (I think due to @Andrej Bauer and @Théo Winterhalter): Nat -> Bool = Nat -> Nat (here = is a defeq) is valid in the cardinal model (take the set-theoretic model, and collapse all sets with the same cardinality). But then we get

(fun x => 0) : Nat -> Bool

and thus

(fun x => 0) 0 : Bool

yet Bool ≠ Nat (and ofc here you can't β-reduce to 0 : Bool either)

But that’s a different flavor of example, right? The propext example gives (True → True) = (Nat → True) in every model of Lean (because it is a theorem), while Nat → Bool = Nat → Nat holds only in some models?

Yes indeed. But even the set-theoretic model satisfies some strange equalities (for instance iirc Empty -> A = Empty -> B for any A and B because both are the empty set?), although again this is not a theorem that holds in all models
(I think both are singletons, but the point stands!)
